newsitem.title: UK: UK rates still seen on hold after Dec jobs data.
newsitem.headline: UK rates still seen on hold after Dec jobs data.

text.p: A fall in UK unemployment in December and steady earnings growth in November will do little to alter expectations the Chancellor will leave interest rates on hold after today's meeting with Bank governor Eddie George, economists said.

"I don't think the data have an impact in the short term," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd. "The tight labour market and prospective upward pressure on wage settlements is a concern longer term, but whether the interest rate increase comes today or in Feburary, it's neutral for that decision."
Unemployment fell by 45,100 in December after a revised plunge of 95,400 in November. Underlying average earnings growth in November was a steady 4.0 percent.
"The markets will find little guidance on UK interest rate policy from today's figures," said CIBC analyst David Coleman.
"The ball is now very firmly in the Chancellor's court. The Bank is likely to push for another modest rise in rates today, but Clarke can make a convincing case for leaving them on hold."
Chancellor Kenneth Clarke is due to meet George at around 1500 GMT amid growing expectations that interest rates will remain on hold at 6.0 percent.
The introduction of the job seekers' allowance continued to distort the data in December, accounting for around 10,000 of the total 45,100 fall.

"Even allowing for distortions caused by the JSA...this constitutes a chunky decline and further emphasises the outperformance of the UK economy versus continental Europe," said Bank America economist Jeremy Hawkins.
Despite the steady decline in unemployment, the tightening labour market has not yet triggered higher pay settlements, as evidenced by the steady average earnings growth in November.

"At some stage the continued declines in unemployment together with a headline inflation rate above three percent will start to put modest upward pressure on wages, although there are no signs of it yet," said Shepperd.
He said there was a risk wage settlements would start to edge up in March or April when many companies conduct their pay rounds.

Average earnings growth has been steady at 4.0 percent for five months and UK employment minister Eric Forth said he expected it to continue to hold at that level. He added he did not believe falling unemployment would prove inflationary.
The Office for National Statistics said the stock of job centre vacancies fell by 1,200 in December, the first decline since January.
HSBC economist Dharshini David said the dip was largely due to the reversal of upward distortions which have plagued the number in recent months.

She said further signs wage inflation pressures were still moderate came from manufacturing unit labour costs growth. This showed a second successive fall in the three months to November of 4.2 percent compared with a year earlier, despite subdued manufacturing output.
